content: This document is an updated Cochrane Review, originally published in 2012, that examines the use of atypical antipsychotics in children and adolescents with disruptive behavior disorders. Disruptive behavior disorders are often treated with atypical antipsychotics, and their use in this population has been increasing. The review specifically aimed to evaluate the effects and safety of individual atypical antipsychotics, rather than the class as a whole, due to differences in pharmacological profiles among these drugs. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing atypical antipsychotics to placebo in children and adolescents aged 18 years or younger with disruptive behavior disorders, including those with comorbid ADHD. The primary outcomes assessed were aggression, conduct problems, and adverse events such as weight gain and metabolic changes. Secondary outcomes included general functioning, social functioning, family functioning, school functioning, parent satisfaction, and noncompliance. The review included 10 trials conducted between 2000 and 2014, involving 896 participants aged 5 to 18 years. Most trials were conducted in outpatient settings. Eight trials evaluated risperidone, one evaluated quetiapine, and one evaluated ziprasidone. Nine trials assessed short-term efficacy (4 to 10 weeks), and one trial evaluated long-term maintenance over six months. The quality of evidence ranged from low to moderate, and nine of the studies received some form of pharmaceutical funding. Primary Outcomes: 1. Aggression: Data from three studies (238 participants) using the Aberrant Behavior Checklist (ABC) Irritability subscale showed that risperidone reduced aggression compared to placebo. The mean difference (MD) was −6.49 points (95% confidence interval [CI]: −8.79 to −4.19), but the evidence quality was low. Two risperidone trials (190 participants) using different scales (Overt Aggression Scale-Modified [OAS-M] and Antisocial Behavior Scale [ABS]) were analyzed. For reactive aggression (ABS Reactive subscale and OAS-M), the standardized mean difference (SMD) was −1.30 (95% CI: −2.21 to −0.40), indicating moderate-quality evidence. For proactive aggression (ABS Proactive subscale and OAS-M), the SMD was −1.12 (95% CI: −2.30 to 0.06), suggesting uncertainty due to overlapping confidence intervals. There was insufficient data to evaluate the effects of quetiapine or ziprasidone on aggression. 2. Conduct Problems: Data from two risperidone trials (225 participants) using the Nisonger Child Behavior Rating Form – Conduct Problem subscale (NCBRF-CP) showed that risperidone reduced conduct problems. The mean score was 8.61 points lower in the risperidone group compared to placebo (95% CI: −11.49 to −5.74), with moderate-quality evidence. 3. Weight Gain: Two trials (138 participants) assessing risperidone alone found that participants gained 2.37 kg more than those on placebo (95% CI: 0.26 to 4.49; moderate-quality evidence). When a trial combining risperidone with stimulant medication was included, participants on the combined treatment gained 2.14 kg more than those on placebo (95% CI: 1.04 to 3.23; low-quality evidence). Secondary Outcomes: Three trials assessed general functioning, social functioning, and parent satisfaction, but no trials evaluated family or school functioning. Data on noncompliance and other adverse events were available from all 10 trials. Authors' Conclusions: Risperidone may reduce aggression and conduct problems in the short term in children and adolescents with disruptive behavior disorders. The reduction in aggression (6.49 points on the ABC Irritability subscale) and conduct problems (8.61 points on the NCBRF-CP) is likely to be clinically significant. However, the clinical significance of findings on reactive versus proactive aggression is less clear, as distinguishing between these subtypes in practice can be challenging. Risperidone is associated with significant weight gain, which is a concern. There is insufficient evidence to support the use of quetiapine, ziprasidone, or other atypical antipsychotics for these disorders. No evidence exists for children under five years of age. The limited number of high-quality trials and the methodological limitations of the current evidence necessitate caution in interpreting these findings. Given the effectiveness of parent-training interventions and the mixed evidence on medication efficacy, atypical antipsychotics should not be used as a standalone treatment. This aligns with current clinical guidelines.
